d.title: SMOTE before the split, and the most seductive number in applied ML
d.caption: Every synthetic row is an interpolation of real minority rows, so when the split comes afterwards the training folds hold near-copies of the test folds' positives. The honest arrangement scores **worse than doing nothing at all** on this problem — which is the finding, not a disappointment.
rows: SMOTE on all rows, then CV

d.title: Six levers for imbalance, and which one actually moved
d.caption: The threshold is almost always the largest single gain — F1 went from 0.109 to 0.351 by moving it, with no change to the model. Most of the other treatments turn out to be a threshold change in disguise, which is why they should be compared against simply tuning the cut.

d.title: Four curve shapes, and what each one tells you to do next
d.caption: A learning curve answers 'would more data help' before you spend anything finding out. The first row is the one people act on wrongly: both lines low and together is **bias**, and more data does nothing — measured at 0.51 to 0.54 across a hundredfold increase in rows.

d.title: Reading a curve in ten seconds
d.caption: Five questions in order, and the first one that answers yes tells you what to do. The last is worth stating explicitly: a validation curve whose two lines are flat across the whole range is telling you the dial does not matter, so stop searching it.

items.label: Is the gap wide?
items.desc: variance: regularise, average, or get data

items.label: Are both lines low and together?
items.desc: bias: capacity or features; data will not help

items.label: Is validation still rising at the right edge?
items.desc: data will help; get it before changing anything

items.label: Both flat and together, at a good level?
items.desc: done; the rest is features or noise

items.label: Is the fold spread wide?
items.desc: the estimate is unreliable: do not tune on it

items.label: Both lines flat across the whole dial?
items.desc: the hyperparameter does not matter; stop searching

d.title: Eight questions that choose the family, with this course's evidence
d.caption: None of these is answered by a leaderboard. The row-count question alone overturns the usual instinct: boosting defaults were the **worst** models on 989 rows, and the four libraries tied at 0.968 on 200,000.

d.title: The estimator contract, and what each method may not do
d.caption: The prohibitions are the content. `__init__` may not validate or transform its arguments — it only stores them — because `clone` rebuilds an estimator from `get_params` and anything computed in the constructor would be silently lost per fold.

d.title: Four ways to persist a model, and what each trusts
d.caption: `joblib.load` **executes whatever the file tells it to** — a model artefact from an untrusted source is a remote-code-execution vector, and one from a trusted source that has been tampered with is the same thing. ONNX is a data-only graph, which is what makes it the format for crossing a trust boundary, and it was 40× faster in the request path here.

d.title: Three axes, and what each choice costs
d.caption: Every method here explains **the model**, not the world. If a leaking refund column were in the features, permutation importance would rank it first — correctly, because the model does rely on it, and it is an effect of churn rather than a cause.

d.title: Why PDP lies when features are correlated, and ALE does not
d.caption: A PDP varies one feature across its whole range while holding the others at their observed values — which constructs rows that cannot exist, and asks the model to extrapolate into them. On a correlated pair the PDP slope came out **1.58 against a true 2.0**. ALE averages local differences within a bin instead, so it never leaves the data.

d.title: Shapley values: why there is only one fair answer
d.caption: Four axioms pin the attribution down uniquely — that is the result that makes SHAP more than one method among many. The price is the marginalisation over every subset, which is why TreeSHAP's exact polynomial-time algorithm for trees mattered so much.

items.label: Efficiency
items.desc: the contributions sum to f(x) minus the base value

items.label: Symmetry
items.desc: two features that always act alike get the same value

items.label: Dummy
items.desc: a feature that never changes the output gets zero

items.label: Additivity
items.desc: values add across an ensemble of models

items.label: These four admit exactly one solution
items.desc: the average marginal contribution over all orderings

items.label: Which costs 2^p subsets in general
items.desc: TreeSHAP computes it exactly, in polynomial time, for trees

d.title: SHAP and LIME are not two implementations of one idea
d.caption: SHAP has a guarantee that its values sum to the prediction; LIME has local fidelity only, and only as measured. The determinism row is the practical one: LIME's top-three features **changed in two of five seeds** on the same row, so a single LIME explanation shown to a customer is not reproducible.

d.caption: A hospital's pen mark on X-rays from the sicker ward; a watermark on one class of stock image; snow behind the huskies; the acquisition channel encoded in a customer id. The cue differs and the procedure does not — and the last test needs no hypothesis at all.

d.title: Attention is not attribution
d.caption: Attention weights say where a representation was **gathered from**, not what moved the output — and the two can disagree completely: a token receiving 85% of the attention had a *negative* contribution to the prediction. The other methods differ mainly in whether they come with a completeness guarantee.

d.title: Every detector is a density estimate in disguise
d.caption: Choosing a detector is choosing which assumption describes 'normal' for your data, and each one's failure mode is a dataset where its assumption is false. That is the whole lesson: a bimodal column defeats the z-score, a curved manifold defeats Mahalanobis, mixed densities defeat the KNN distance.

cells.text: hard to isolate by random cuts

d.title: Masking: the second outlier hides the first
d.caption: The series 10, 11, 12, 10, 11, 13, 12, 50, 52. Grubbs' test gives the 52 a G of 1.82 against a critical 2.22 — **not flagged**, because the 50 has pushed the standard deviation to 17.5. Remove the 52 by other means and the 50 is flagged immediately. The modified z-score flags both at once, because the median of 12 and the MAD of 1 never moved.

d.title: contamination='auto' is not a sensible default
d.caption: With `contamination='auto'` scikit-learn sets the offset to −0.5, so every row whose path is shorter than a random point's expectation is predicted anomalous — **176 of 1,004 rows, 17.5%, for four planted anomalies**. The score distribution's centre depends on the data's shape and dimension, not on how many anomalies it holds. The ranking is unaffected: Spearman 1.000 between contamination 0.01 and 0.1, because it is the same forest with a different offset.

d.title: Setting a threshold when there are no labels
d.caption: Without labels there is no optimum to find, so the threshold must come from somewhere outside the data — and review capacity is the honest answer in almost every production system. The random audit sample is the part that is usually missing: without it the base rate is unknown, and a supervised model trained on the queue learns only the queue's biases.
